lessons.title: The exception hierarchy
lessons.summary: Throwable, Error, checked vs unchecked, and who throws what.

blocks.text: When Java hits a problem it can't continue from, it **throws** an exception: an object describing what went wrong. If nobody **catches** it, the program stops and prints a stack trace.

blocks.caption: The JVM throws, nobody catches, main ends.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: `try/except` in Python becomes `try/catch` in Java. The big difference: for **checked** exceptions, the Java **compiler** forces you to deal with them. Python never checks this.
Every exception class extends `Throwable`. Two branches matter:

blocks.code:
Throwable
├─ Error              unchecked
│  └─ StackOverflowError, OutOfMemoryError
└─ Exception          checked
   ├─ IOException, SQLException ...
   └─ RuntimeException  unchecked
      └─ NullPointerException ...

rows: JVM is in trouble; don't catch
usually a bug in the code

blocks.title: RuntimeException is an Exception
blocks.text: `RuntimeException` **extends** `Exception`, yet it's unchecked. `catch (Exception e)` catches runtime exceptions too. `Error` is **not** an `Exception`, so `catch (Exception e)` does not catch a `StackOverflowError`.

blocks.title: Beyond the core objectives: assert
blocks.text: `assert count > 0 : "empty";` checks a condition only when the JVM runs with `-ea` (enable assertions). If it's false, it throws an `AssertionError` (an `Error`) with the message. Without `-ea` the statement is skipped entirely.

steps.prompt: Which of these is a checked exception?
steps.explanation: `IOException` extends `Exception` but not `RuntimeException`, so it's checked. NPE and `ArithmeticException` are runtime exceptions; `StackOverflowError` is an `Error`. Both of those groups are unchecked.

steps.prompt: Which two are unchecked exceptions? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `IllegalArgumentException` and `ClassCastException` extend `RuntimeException`, so they're unchecked. `Exception` itself is checked, and so are `IOException` and its subclass `FileNotFoundException`.

blocks.text: For a **checked** exception, the compiler insists on one of two things wherever it can be thrown:

items: **Handle** it: wrap the call in `try/catch`.
**Declare** it: add `throws IOException` to your method, passing the duty to your caller.

blocks.text: Unchecked exceptions (runtime exceptions and errors) are free: you may catch or declare them, but you don't have to.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `b()` calls `load()`, which declares the checked `IOException`, but `b()` neither catches it nor declares it. `a()` is fine: `throws Exception` covers `IOException` because it's a superclass.

blocks.text: Know these by heart. Some are thrown by the **JVM** itself, others by **code** (yours or the Java API) with `throw`.

blocks.title: Family links
blocks.text: `NumberFormatException` extends `IllegalArgumentException`. `FileNotFoundException` extends `IOException`. Both facts show up in catch-order questions.

blocks.title: Only ints divide by zero badly
blocks.text: `10 / 0` throws `ArithmeticException`, but `10.0 / 0` is `Infinity`. Floating-point math never throws.

blocks.title: UncheckedIOException isn't an IOException
blocks.text: `UncheckedIOException` wraps an `IOException` but extends `RuntimeException`. The two types are unrelated, so `catch (IOException | UncheckedIOException e)` is legal.

steps.explanation: `"12a"` is not a valid int, so `Integer.parseInt` throws `NumberFormatException` (an unchecked `IllegalArgumentException`). It compiles fine because the exception is unchecked.
The cast compiles because `Object` could hold an `Integer`. At runtime the object is a `String`, so the JVM throws `ClassCastException`.
Floating-point division by zero gives `Infinity` and prints `Infinity`. Only integer division (and `%`) by zero throws `ArithmeticException`.

options: Error is a checked exception and must be declared.
Error and Exception both extend Throwable.
A catch block can't catch an Error.
steps.explanation: `Throwable` has two direct branches: `Error` and `Exception`. `Error` is unchecked but not a `RuntimeException`. You *can* catch an `Error` (`catch (Error e)` or `catch (Throwable t)`), you just usually shouldn't.

lessons.title: try, catch and finally
lessons.summary: Which blocks run, in which order, and who wins a return.

blocks.caption: Prints ACDE

items: `try` runs until a statement throws. The rest of `try` is **skipped** (no `B`).
The **first** `catch` whose type matches runs.
`finally` runs **always**: after a normal `try`, after a `catch`, even when nothing catches.
A `try` needs at least one `catch` or a `finally`. Braces are required.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Same idea as `try/except/finally`. Java has no `else:` block, and `catch` must name a type: there's no bare `except:`.

steps.explanation: `s.length()` throws an NPE. The only catch is for `ArithmeticException`, so it doesn't match. `finally` still prints `3`, then the NPE leaves `main`, so `4` is never printed.

blocks.text: Catch blocks are checked top to bottom. If a superclass comes first, a later subclass catch can never run. Java treats that as **unreachable code**, a compile error.

blocks.title: Unreachable catch
blocks.text: Superclass before subclass = **does not compile**. Unrelated types (like `ArithmeticException` and `NullPointerException`) can be in any order.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `NumberFormatException` is a subclass of `IllegalArgumentException`, which is already caught on line 3, so the catch on line 5 is unreachable. `RuntimeException` after them is fine: it's broader.
Subclass first is legal. Only the **first** matching catch runs (`NFE`), then `finally` (`F`). A thrown exception is never handled by two catch blocks.

blocks.text: `finally` runs even when `try` or `catch` executes `return`. The return value is computed first, then `finally` runs, then the method returns.

blocks.title: return in finally wins
blocks.text: A `return` inside `finally` replaces the earlier return value, and even swallows a thrown exception. Legal, terrible style, popular on the exam.

steps.explanation: `return x;` saves the value 20. `finally` then sets `x` to 30 and prints `30 `. Changing a local primitive in `finally` doesn't change the saved return value, so `main` prints `20`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The catch block prepares to return `"catch"`, but `finally` runs before the method returns and its `return "finally"` replaces it.

items: `System.exit(...)` stops the JVM at once. `finally` does **not** run.
If the JVM crashes or the machine loses power, nothing runs.
If `finally` itself throws, that exception **replaces** the one in flight. The original is lost.

blocks.caption: Prints only A

steps.prompt: A finally block runs even if the try block calls System.exit(0).
steps.explanation: `System.exit` terminates the JVM immediately, so the `finally` block is skipped. It's the classic exception to "finally always runs".

steps.prompt: Complete the code with the right keywords.
steps.explanation: Java uses `try`, `catch` and `finally`. `except` is Python, `throws` belongs in a method declaration, and `final` is a modifier, not `finally`.

options: abc, then a RuntimeException is thrown
ab, then a RuntimeException is thrown
steps.explanation: The `IllegalStateException` is caught (`b`). The catch block throws a new `RuntimeException`, which no catch in this statement handles, but `finally` still runs first (`c`). Then the exception leaves `main`.

lessons.title: Multi-catch
lessons.summary: Catch several types in one block with |, and its three rules.

blocks.text: When different exceptions need the same handling, list them with `|`:

blocks.caption: Prints 2, bad: x, bad: 0

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python writes `except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError) as e:`. Java uses `|` between types and one variable name **at the end**.

items: The types must **not** be related by inheritance: `FileNotFoundException | IOException` doesn't compile (just catch `IOException`).
Only **one** variable name, after the last type: `catch (A e | B e)` doesn't compile.
The variable is implicitly **final**: `e = ...;` doesn't compile.
Inside the block, `e` has the closest common supertype, so you can only call methods of that type.

blocks.title: Redundant types are errors
blocks.text: In a multi-catch, a subclass next to its superclass is a **compile error**, not a harmless duplicate.

steps.prompt: The try block calls a method declared `throws IOException`. Which two catch clauses compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Options 2 and 5 list unrelated types (`NumberFormatException` extends `IllegalArgumentException`, not `IllegalStateException`). Options 1 and 4 pair a subclass with its superclass. Option 3 repeats the variable name, which isn't allowed.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: A multi-catch parameter is implicitly final, so assigning to `e` on line 7 is a compile error. The type list itself is fine: the two types are unrelated.
The multi-catch matches the actual exception, an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. `getClass()` reports the runtime class of the object, not the declared type of `e`.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Expect to be asked whether `e = new ...;` compiles. Check whether the catch has one type (yes) or several (no).

steps.prompt: In a single-type catch such as `catch (IOException e)`, the statement `e = new IOException();` compiles.
steps.explanation: Only a **multi-catch** parameter is implicitly final. A single-type catch parameter can be reassigned. It's legal, just bad style.

steps.prompt: Which statement compiles inside this catch block?
steps.explanation: Rethrowing `e` is fine: its type is the common supertype `RuntimeException`, which is unchecked. `e` is final, so `e = null` fails. `e` might be an `ArithmeticException`, so it can't be assigned to `NumberFormatException` without a cast. Exceptions have no `length()` method.
Multi-catch uses a single `|` between types (not `||` or a comma) and one variable name after the last type.

lessons.title: throw, throws and chaining
lessons.summary: Throwing, declaring, rethrowing and wrapping exceptions.

blocks.title: Unreachable after throw
blocks.text: `throw` always ends the block. A statement right after it in the same block is unreachable: **compile error**. Also, `throw IOException;` doesn't compile: you need an object, `throw new IOException();`.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `raise` is Java's `throw`. Python has no equivalent of `throws`.

steps.explanation: The declaration uses `throws` (plural, lists types). The statement uses `throw` followed by an exception object. `raise` is Python.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: The `throw` on line 6 always runs, so line 7 can never be reached: unreachable statement. The `throw` inside the `if` on line 4 is fine because the `if` might be false.

blocks.text: If a `try` block can't possibly throw a **checked** exception, catching it is a compile error. Unchecked types, `Exception` and `Throwable` are always allowed, because they also cover runtime exceptions.

blocks.title: Subclasses count
blocks.text: A method that `throws IOException` might throw a `FileNotFoundException`, so catching the subclass is allowed. But then `IOException` itself still needs handling.

steps.prompt: The try block contains only `System.out.println("x");`. Which two exception types can its catch block name without a compile error? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `IllegalStateException` is unchecked, so it may always be caught. `Exception` is allowed because it includes runtime exceptions. The checked types (`IOException`, `FileNotFoundException`, `InterruptedException`) can't be thrown by `println`, so catching them doesn't compile.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Catching `FileNotFoundException` is allowed (it could be thrown, being a subclass of `IOException`). But `m()` declares `IOException`, which is broader and still unhandled, so line 7 doesn't compile.

blocks.text: Often you catch a low-level exception and throw a more meaningful one. Pass the original as the **cause** so nothing is lost:

blocks.caption: Prints bad config, then NumberFormatException

blocks.title: Beyond the core objectives: logging
blocks.text: With `java.util.logging`, `logger.log(Level.WARNING, "load failed", e)` attaches the exception so its stack trace is printed. A record is published only if it passes **both** the Logger's level and the Handler's level. Order: `FINEST < FINER < FINE < CONFIG < INFO < WARNING < SEVERE`.

steps.explanation: Printing an exception calls `toString()`: the **fully qualified runtime class**, a colon, and the message. The declared catch type (`RuntimeException`) doesn't matter.

blocks.text: If you `catch (Exception e)` and just `throw e;`, the compiler remembers which checked exceptions the try block could actually throw. The method only needs to declare those, as long as `e` is never reassigned.

steps.explanation: This is a precise rethrow: the try block can only throw `IOException` (checked) or unchecked exceptions, and `e` is effectively final, so `throws IOException` is enough. The `IOException` travels to `main`, which prints its message.

lessons.title: try-with-resources
lessons.summary: Automatic closing, close order, scope and suppressed exceptions.

blocks.text: Files, sockets and database connections must be **closed**. Declare them in parentheses after `try` and Java closes them for you, even when an exception is thrown.
`Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable`. A resource must implement one of them, or the code doesn't compile.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: This is Java's `with open('a.txt') as f:`. The resource variable is declared in the `try (...)` header.
Resources are closed in **reverse** order of declaration, and **before** any `catch` or `finally` block runs.

verify.value:
open A
open B
body
close B
close A
catch
finally

blocks.title: Already closed in catch
blocks.text: By the time `catch` runs, the resources are already closed. That's why the resource variables aren't even in scope there.

steps.prompt: Put the output of the program above in order.
steps.explanation: Resources open in declaration order and close in **reverse** order (B before A). Closing happens right after the body, before `catch` and `finally`.

verify.value:
open A
open B
body
close B
close A
catch
finally

steps.prompt: The constructor of the second resource throws. What is the output?
steps.explanation: `A` opens. Creating `B` throws, so the body never runs. Only resources that were successfully created are closed, so `A` is closed, then the catch runs.

items: The resource variable's scope is the `try` block only, not `catch` or `finally`.
Resource variables declared in the header are implicitly `final`.
Since Java 9 you can use an existing variable, if it's `final` or effectively final: `try (in) { ... }`.
Unlike a plain `try`, try-with-resources needs **no** catch or finally.
Separate resources with `;`. A trailing `;` after the last one is allowed.

blocks.title: close() throws Exception
blocks.text: If your class implements `AutoCloseable` and keeps `close() throws Exception`, every try-with-resources using it must handle or declare `Exception`, even with an empty body.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Line 5 reassigns `r`, so `r` is not effectively final. A variable used as a resource in `try (r)` must be final or effectively final, so line 2 fails.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about try-with-resources are true? Choose two.
options: Resources are closed in the reverse order of declaration.
Resources are closed after the catch block runs.
A try-with-resources statement must have a catch or finally block.
A resource variable can be used in the finally block.
A resource must implement AutoCloseable, directly or through Closeable.
steps.explanation: Closing happens in reverse order, **before** catch and finally. The resource is out of scope in catch and finally. Catch and finally are optional for try-with-resources. Resources must be `AutoCloseable`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The scope of `s` is only the try block. Using it in `finally` on line 5 is a compile error. (It would be pointless anyway: the Scanner is already closed.)

blocks.text: What if the body throws **and** `close()` throws? The body's exception is the **primary** one. The close exception is attached to it as **suppressed**, so `catch` sees the primary.

blocks.caption: Prints body, then close

blocks.title: Only close throws?
blocks.text: If the body finishes normally and only `close()` throws, the close exception becomes the primary exception, with nothing suppressed.

blocks.title: Plain finally loses exceptions
blocks.text: Suppression is a try-with-resources feature. If a plain `finally` block throws, it simply replaces the first exception.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The body completes normally (`body `). Then `close()` throws, and that exception is the primary one, caught by the catch block. Nothing was suppressed, so `getSuppressed().length` is 0.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `Door.close()` declares `throws Exception`. The implicit `close()` call happens in `main`, which neither catches nor declares `Exception`, so line 8 doesn't compile. Fix it by declaring `close()` without `throws`, or by handling `Exception`.

lessons.title: Custom exceptions
lessons.summary: Write your own checked or unchecked exception classes.

blocks.text: Extend `Exception` for a **checked** exception, or `RuntimeException` for an **unchecked** one.

items: By convention, the name ends in `Exception`.
Constructors are **not** inherited. Write the ones you need and pass the arguments on with `super(...)`.
Usual constructors: `()`, `(String message)`, `(String message, Throwable cause)`, `(Throwable cause)`.

blocks.title: Checked or unchecked?
blocks.text: Choose checked when the caller can reasonably recover (account has no funds). Choose unchecked for programming errors (invalid argument).

options: An AgeException is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `AgeException` extends `Exception`, so it's checked. `check` throws it on line 4 without declaring `throws AgeException`, so the code doesn't compile.

steps.prompt: A custom exception that extends RuntimeException must be declared with throws by methods that throw it.
steps.explanation: Subclasses of `RuntimeException` are unchecked. Declaring them is optional: the compiler never requires it.

blocks.text: `getMessage()` returns whatever you passed to `super(msg)`. With the no-arg constructor it returns `null`.

blocks.title: No free constructors
blocks.text: If your class only defines `AppException(String, Throwable)`, then `new AppException("x")` and `new AppException()` don't compile. Once you write any constructor, there's no default one.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The no-arg constructor doesn't pass a message to the superclass, so `getMessage()` returns `null`, and `println` prints `null`.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `MyEx` only declares a `(String)` constructor. Constructors aren't inherited from `RuntimeException`, and no default constructor exists once you write one, so `new MyEx()` fails.

Exception classes are classes, so you `extends` them (`implements` is for interfaces). `super(m, c)` passes the message and cause to `Exception`. `this(m, c)` would call the same constructor again, a compile error.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about custom exceptions are true? Choose two.
options: A class that extends Exception, but not RuntimeException, is a checked exception.
A custom exception inherits all constructors of its superclass.
A custom exception must override getMessage().
Passing a cause to super(message, cause) makes it available through getCause().
A custom exception can't extend RuntimeException.
steps.explanation: Being checked depends only on the superclass. Constructors are never inherited. `getMessage()` already works without overriding. Extending `RuntimeException` is the normal way to make an unchecked custom exception.
The NPE is caught and wrapped: `DataException` gets the message `load` and the NPE as its cause, so `getCause()` returns the `NullPointerException`.

lessons.title: Exceptions, overriding and constructors
lessons.summary: What overriding methods and constructors may throw.

blocks.text: An overriding method may **not** throw new or broader **checked** exceptions than the method it overrides. It **may**:

items: throw the same checked exceptions,
throw narrower ones (subclasses),
throw fewer, or none at all,
throw any unchecked exception.

blocks.text: Why? Code written for `Animal` only handles `IOException`. If a `Cat` could throw any `Exception`, that code would break.

steps.prompt: Given `class A { void run() throws IOException { } }`, which three methods compile in `class B extends A`? Choose three.
steps.explanation: Throwing nothing, a subclass (`EOFException` extends `IOException`), or an unchecked exception is fine. `Exception` is broader, and `InterruptedException` is a new checked exception. `private` reduces access, which overriding never allows.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Implementing an interface method follows the same rule as overriding. `FileNotFoundException` is narrower than `IOException`: fine. `Exception` on line 9 is broader: compile error.

blocks.text: The compiler looks at the **declared** type of the reference, not the object, to decide which exceptions a call can throw.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: If a subclass removes the `throws` clause, calling through a **superclass** reference still requires handling the superclass's checked exceptions.

options: An IOException is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `Sub.go()` throws nothing, but `b` is declared as `Base`, whose `go()` declares `IOException`. `main` doesn't handle it, so line 10 doesn't compile.

blocks.text: Constructors work the **other way round**. A subclass constructor calls `super()`, and it can't catch an exception from that call (nothing may come before `super()`). So it must declare the same or **broader** exceptions.
An exception thrown while a class's **static** initialization runs is wrapped in an `ExceptionInInitializerError`.

blocks.caption: ExceptionInInitializerError, caused by NumberFormatException

blocks.text: The class is then marked as **failed**. Its initializer is never retried: every later use throws `NoClassDefFoundError`.

blocks.title: Opposite rules
blocks.text: Overriding methods: same or **narrower** checked exceptions. Subclass constructors: same or **broader**. A class with no constructor gets a default one that doesn't compile if the parent's no-arg constructor throws a checked exception.

steps.prompt: Given `class Parent { Parent() throws IOException { } }`, which constructor compiles in `class Child extends Parent`?
steps.explanation: `Child()` implicitly calls `super()`, which can throw `IOException`. The constructor can't catch it, so it must declare `IOException` or something broader, like `Exception`. Narrower or unchecked types don't cover it.

options: An ExceptionInInitializerError is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The static initializer of `Config` throws `NumberFormatException` when the class is first used. The JVM wraps it in an `ExceptionInInitializerError` (with the NFE as its cause).

steps.prompt: An overriding method may declare `throws IllegalArgumentException` even if the overridden method declares no exceptions.
steps.explanation: The overriding rule only restricts **checked** exceptions. `IllegalArgumentException` is unchecked, so it may be added freely.

options: `throw` is followed by an exception object; `throws` by one or more exception types.
